statements.quote: The *Brief History of AI* and *The Mind That Built Machines* told the story one way: the brain came first, and the machine was assembled from its parts.
statements.section: Two Machines, One Mirror

statements.quote: But the mirror now works **both** ways, and this chapter is about the full reflection.
statements.section: Two Machines, One Mirror

statements.quote: In the first half, the body's own measured laws — the all-or-none spike, the charge-up-and-fire membrane, the retina's contrast circuit, the rule of synaptic strengthening — became the machine's building blocks.
statements.section: Two Machines, One Mirror

statements.quote: In the second half, the turnarounds of the last decade: deep networks that now model the visual cortex better than any hand-built theory, foundation models that predict a brain's responses, and decoders that read the movie from the fMRI.
statements.section: Two Machines, One Mirror

statements.quote: Same mathematics, two directions.
statements.section: Two Machines, One Mirror

statements.quote: Before there was a "neural network" there was a **neuron** — and nearly every load-bearing noun in the field is a loanword from a nineteenth-century anatomist.
statements.section: I. The Vocabulary Was Stolen From Neurology

statements.quote: \marginfig{cajal_cerebellum.jpg}{Santiago Ramón y Cajal's stained cerebellum, c.
statements.section: I. The Vocabulary Was Stolen From Neurology

statements.quote: 1905 — the real cell, and the word it lent the field.}
statements.section: I. The Vocabulary Was Stolen From Neurology

statements.quote: \citeauthorlastnameand{cajal1888} used \citeauthor{golgi1873}'s silver stain to show the nervous system is a population of *separate cells* passing messages across gaps — the **neuron doctrine**, traced in detail in the *Untold History* chapter \cite{cajal1888} \cite{waldeyer1891}; \citeauthorlastnameand{waldeyer1891} named the cells in 1891.
statements.section: I. The Vocabulary Was Stolen From Neurology

statements.quote: Once the noun exists, the grammar follows.
statements.section: I. The Vocabulary Was Stolen From Neurology

statements.quote: A **synapse** is the gap; a **weight** its strength.
statements.section: I. The Vocabulary Was Stolen From Neurology

statements.quote: A **layer** is a slice of the **cortex**, which is built in layers.
statements.section: I. The Vocabulary Was Stolen From Neurology

statements.quote: **Learning** is **plasticity**, the documented habit of re-weighting synapses.
statements.section: I. The Vocabulary Was Stolen From Neurology

statements.quote: A **receptive field** is the patch of world a visual cell watches \cite{hubelwiesel}.
statements.section: I. The Vocabulary Was Stolen From Neurology

statements.quote: Even a neuron that "fires, or doesn't" just names a cell that spikes or stays quiet.
statements.section: I. The Vocabulary Was Stolen From Neurology

statements.quote: The aha is small but total: **the language of machine learning is a dialect of neurology.** ML researchers did not invent "neuron", "synapse", "layer", "weight", or "learning".
statements.section: I. The Vocabulary Was Stolen From Neurology

statements.quote: They found those words already in a Madrid laboratory in the 1880s, and built the machine out of the vocabulary they borrowed.
statements.section: I. The Vocabulary Was Stolen From Neurology

statements.quote: The *Brief History of AI* gives the timeline; the deeper point is that the first machines were not metaphors *for* the brain but literal formalizations of three documented physiological laws.
statements.section: II. The First Machines Were Built on the Body's Own Laws

statements.quote: **The all-or-none spike became the binary neuron.** A single nerve fiber, once its stimulus crosses threshold, fires one impulse of fixed size — or nothing at all; the strength of the signal is carried by the *rate* of firing, not its size.
statements.section: II. The First Machines Were Built on the Body's Own Laws

statements.quote: That law, the **all-or-none principle**, was established for sensory nerves by \citeauthorlastnameand{adrian1922allornothing} in the 1920s \cite{adrian1922allornothing}.
statements.section: II. The First Machines Were Built on the Body's Own Laws

statements.quote: In 1943 \citeauthorlastnameand{mccullochpitts1943} took that law, added the **refractory period** (the brief inexcitable gap after each spike) and a fixed synaptic delay, and turned the nerve into a binary, once-per-time-step unit — then proved a network of such units computes any Boolean function \cite{mccullochpitts1943}.
statements.section: II. The First Machines Were Built on the Body's Own Laws

statements.quote: The "neuron" inside every network since is a formal model of the action potential, not an analogy to it.
statements.section: II. The First Machines Were Built on the Body's Own Laws

statements.quote: **The membrane became the integrator.** Thirty-six years earlier, \citeauthor{lapicque1907} had modeled the excitable membrane as a capacitor that charges until it crosses a threshold and then resets — the **integrate-and-fire** neuron \cite{lapicque1907}.
statements.section: II. The First Machines Were Built on the Body's Own Laws

statements.quote: It was the first *quantitative* model of a nerve, and it is the direct ancestor of every spiking network.
statements.section: II. The First Machines Were Built on the Body's Own Laws

statements.quote: \marginfig{mark_i_perceptron_manual.png}{The Mark I Perceptron, 1958: motor-driven potentiometers whose resistance *was* the weight — the first machine built entirely from borrowed vocabulary (\cite[Mark I Perceptron, operator's manual]{mark_i_perceptron_manual}).}
statements.section: II. The First Machines Were Built on the Body's Own Laws

statements.quote: **The retina's contrast circuit became winner-take-all.** In the eye, an excited receptor *suppresses its neighbors*, sharpening edges — **lateral inhibition**, recorded from the horseshoe-crab retina by \citeauthorlastnameand{hartline1956limulus} \cite{hartline1956limulus} \cite{lateral_inhibition_wiki}.
statements.section: II. The First Machines Were Built on the Body's Own Laws

statements.quote: The rule "the strongest unit wins, the rest go quiet" is exactly **competitive, winner-take-all** dynamics \cite{winner_take_all_wiki} — the hard version of the soft max that closes a network's output today.
statements.section: II. The First Machines Were Built on the Body's Own Laws

statements.quote: **The receptive field became the convolution.** Hartline had also shown an optic fiber responds to a *patch* of the visual field — the **receptive field** \cite{hartline1956limulus} \cite{hubelwiesel}; \citeauthorlastnameand{hubelwiesel} mapped that idea up through the cortex, and \citeauthor{neocognitron} and \citeauthor{lecun1989backpropagation} turned it into the convolution (the full story is in *What Machines See*).
statements.section: II. The First Machines Were Built on the Body's Own Laws

statements.quote: **One sentence became the learning rule.** In 1949 \citeauthor{hebb1949organizationofbehaviour} wrote that neurons which fire together strengthen their connection \cite{hebb1949organizationofbehaviour}; sharpened by an error signal — the *Brief History* shows the math — that intuition is the learning rule.
statements.section: II. The First Machines Were Built on the Body's Own Laws

statements.quote: The aha: the first machine was not *inspired by* the brain.
statements.section: II. The First Machines Were Built on the Body's Own Laws

statements.quote: It was built **from** the brain's own, measured, laws.
statements.section: II. The First Machines Were Built on the Body's Own Laws

statements.quote: If the cell became the unit, the *maps* the brain builds became the model's memory.
statements.section: III. The World Inside the Head

statements.quote: **The cognitive map.** \citeauthorlastnameand{okeefe1971place} recorded neurons in a rat's hippocampus that fire only in a particular place — **place cells**, whose fields tile the environment into a map \cite{okeefe1971place}.
statements.section: III. The World Inside the Head

statements.quote: The Mosers added **grid cells**, a hexagonal lattice beneath them, and the three shared the 2014 Nobel for the brain's "GPS" \cite{nobel2014spatial}.
statements.section: III. The World Inside the Head

statements.quote: Then \citeauthorlastnameand{stachenfeld2017predictivemap} showed the hippocampus does not just log where you *are* but *predicts where you will go* — a model of the environment used to plan \cite{stachenfeld2017predictivemap}.
statements.section: III. The World Inside the Head

statements.quote: The "world model" AI now learns at billion-dollar scale was already in the brain's vocabulary.
statements.section: III. The World Inside the Head

statements.quote: **The working-memory bottleneck becomes the context window.** The mind holds only about four — not seven, as \citeauthor{miller1956magicalnumber} claimed — distinct items at once \cite{miller1956magicalnumber} \cite{cowan2001magical4}, and \citeauthor{baddeley1986workingmemory} mapped that cramped scratch space \cite{baddeley1986workingmemory}.
statements.section: III. The World Inside the Head

statements.quote: A tiny buffer is the constraint that *forces* a mind to compress and chunk — which the Mind chapter showed is the origin of the token.
statements.section: III. The World Inside the Head

statements.quote: A model's context window is a hippocampal scratchpad: small, and empty the moment the conversation ends.
statements.section: III. The World Inside the Head

statements.quote: **Sleep becomes offline training.** The map and the memory are consolidated overnight; \citeauthorlastnameand{diekelmann2010sleep} and others documented memories replayed and stabilized during sleep, the hippocampus running the day's sequences fast-forward in the dark \cite{diekelmann2010sleep}.
statements.section: III. The World Inside the Head

statements.quote: The brain fine-tunes at night.
statements.section: III. The World Inside the Head

statements.quote: A model that replays and consolidates overnight is, at last, doing what the hippocampus does.
statements.section: III. The World Inside the Head

statements.quote: The deepest overlap is not a metaphor but an equation.
statements.section: IV. Where the Math Coincides: The Cortex as a Predictive Machine

statements.quote: In the **predictive-coding** picture, \citeauthorlastnameand{rao1999predictive} showed the visual cortex works top-down: higher areas send a *prediction*, lower areas send back only the *mismatch* \cite{rao1999predictive} — a generative model minimizing a loss, where the loss is just the gap between what the senses deliver and what the model forecast:
statements.section: IV. Where the Math Coincides: The Cortex as a Predictive Machine

statements.quote: \citeauthor{clark2013whatevernext} generalized this to the whole brain \cite{clark2013whatevernext}, and \citeauthorlastnameand{keller2018canonical} and \citeauthorlastnameand{bastos2012microcircuit} have since pinned the down-prediction / up-error pattern onto real cortical microcircuitry \cite{keller2018canonical} \cite{bastos2012microcircuit}.
statements.section: IV. Where the Math Coincides: The Cortex as a Predictive Machine

statements.quote: In 2023, \citeauthorlastnameand{caucheteux2023predictive} fit a hierarchical predictive-coding model to human MEG while people listened to speech, and it accounted for how the auditory hierarchy builds up the representation step by step \cite{caucheteux2023predictive} — a brain theory and a learning algorithm that are, in that fit, literally the same object.
statements.section: IV. Where the Math Coincides: The Cortex as a Predictive Machine

statements.quote: And the algorithm at the heart of this course — **backpropagation** — may itself be a brain mechanism.
statements.section: IV. Where the Math Coincides: The Cortex as a Predictive Machine

statements.quote: \citeauthorlastnameand{whittington2019backprop} asked how a nervous system could push an error signal *backwards* through a hierarchy, the one step no obvious biological wire seems to do \cite{whittington2019backprop}.
statements.section: IV. Where the Math Coincides: The Cortex as a Predictive Machine

statements.quote: But the tool that built the mirror may have been found in the brain first.
statements.section: IV. Where the Math Coincides: The Cortex as a Predictive Machine

statements.quote: For a century the current ran one way — brain to machine.
statements.section: V. How the Machine Started Shaping the Brain

statements.quote: The last decade reversed it.
statements.section: V. How the Machine Started Shaping the Brain

statements.quote: **The machine became the brain's best model.** \citeauthor{kriegeskorte2015dcnn} argued that a pretrained deep convolutional network is now the best computational model of the primate visual ventral stream \cite{kriegeskorte2015dcnn} — that systems neuroscientists now reach for a deep net the way an earlier generation reached for a linear filter.
statements.section: V. How the Machine Started Shaping the Brain

statements.quote: The architecture built to read handwritten digits is now the lens for reading the cortex.
statements.section: V. How the Machine Started Shaping the Brain

statements.quote: **The brain became a foundation model.** Wang and colleagues trained one large model on neural recordings and showed it predicts a single mouse's visual-cortex responses to *novel* stimulus types it never saw during training — zero-shot \cite{wang2025foundation}.
statements.section: V. How the Machine Started Shaping the Brain

statements.quote: The "foundation model" paradigm, transplanted from language, now predicts a brain.
statements.section: V. How the Machine Started Shaping the Brain

statements.quote: **The machine reads the experience.** In 2011, a team led by Shinji Nishimoto reconstructed the actual *movie* a person had watched from fMRI in visual cortex \cite{nishimoto2011reconstruct}.
statements.section: V. How the Machine Started Shaping the Brain

statements.quote: Huth and colleagues fit a single model to how natural speech activates the whole cortex \cite{huth2016semanticmaps}.
statements.section: V. How the Machine Started Shaping the Brain

statements.quote: Affolter and colleagues decoded the specific word a person was reading and fed it to a language model to finish the sentence \cite{affolter2020brain2word}.
statements.section: V. How the Machine Started Shaping the Brain

statements.quote: By 2025, fMRI was being turned straight into text with a language model on the other end \cite{lu2025fmritotext}.
statements.section: V. How the Machine Started Shaping the Brain

statements.quote: The field now builds the data to do this at scale \cite{allen2022nsd}.
statements.section: V. How the Machine Started Shaping the Brain

statements.quote: **The brain became the machine's teacher.** Schwartz and colleagues fine-tuned a transformer until its internal representations *predicted human brain activity* — and the model that best fit the brain got better at language too \cite{schwartz2019brainbias}.
statements.section: V. How the Machine Started Shaping the Brain

statements.quote: And the alignment runs deeper than a correlation: Hosseini and colleagues found that the *structure* of the representational space — not just its statistics — is shared between biological and artificial networks \cite{hosseini2024universality}.
statements.section: V. How the Machine Started Shaping the Brain

statements.quote: **The brain became the yardstick.** Even how a machine's intelligence is judged is set by the brain: the field's benchmarks are increasingly framed not around beating an adult expert but around matching the flexible, data-efficient learning of a young child from a trickle of unlabeled examples.
statements.section: V. How the Machine Started Shaping the Brain

statements.quote: The aha: the machine is no longer just built *from* the brain — it is now the instrument the brain is measured **with**.
statements.section: V. How the Machine Started Shaping the Brain

statements.quote: The most useful thing the comparison does is mark where the reflection breaks — the places where the two machines genuinely differ.
statements.section: VI. The Divergence: What the Mirror Refuses to Show

statements.quote: There are places the **brain beats the machine**.
statements.section: VI. The Divergence: What the Mirror Refuses to Show

statements.quote: **Energy** is the sharpest: your whole mind runs on about twenty watts, not a data centre.
statements.section: VI. The Divergence: What the Mirror Refuses to Show

statements.quote: **Grounding**: your concepts are tied to a body that can be hurt — the symbol-grounding problem no model has solved.
statements.section: VI. The Divergence: What the Mirror Refuses to Show

statements.quote: And the **"aha"**: the answer that surfaces when you stop looking, the slow offline search the Mind chapter ties to the default-mode network \cite{raichle2007defaultmode}.
statements.section: VI. The Divergence: What the Mirror Refuses to Show

statements.quote: (Learning is *not* on this list — modern models already do one-shot and even zero-shot learning from context; they just do it in a very different way from a hippocampus.) And places the **machine beats the brain**: exact recall, scale, tireless uptime, and the willingness to *optimize*, where a human mind only **satisfices** — settles for good enough \cite{simon1955bounded}.
statements.section: VI. The Divergence: What the Mirror Refuses to Show

statements.quote: That divergence is the map of what you are.
statements.section: VI. The Divergence: What the Mirror Refuses to Show

statements.quote: Where the brain wins, you are *more than a model*; where the machine wins, you are, unavoidably, **bounded**.
statements.section: VI. The Divergence: What the Mirror Refuses to Show

statements.quote: Pull the thread back to the reader.
statements.section: VII. The Mirror on You

statements.quote: The claims above are not about a machine in a data centre.
statements.section: VII. The Mirror on You

statements.quote: They are about the head on the other end of the screen:
statements.section: VII. The Mirror on You

statements.quote: - Your **perception** is a prediction, revised by whatever surprises it \cite{rao1999predictive} \cite{clark2013whatevernext}.
statements.section: VII. The Mirror on You

statements.quote: - Your **reward system** is a reinforcement learner, firing on the gap between what you wanted and what you got \cite{schultz1997dopamine}.
statements.section: VII. The Mirror on You

statements.quote: - Your **memory** is a lossy compression, consolidated overnight \cite{diekelmann2010sleep}.
statements.section: VII. The Mirror on You

statements.quote: - Your **sense of self** is a broadcast — a handful of "winning" ideas promoted to a shared stage the rest of the mind can read \cite{baars} \cite{dehaene}.
statements.section: VII. The Mirror on You

statements.quote: - Your **"aha"** is a background process — the default-mode network doing its slow search while the foreground is busy \cite{raichle2007defaultmode}.
statements.section: VII. The Mirror on You

statements.quote: \marginfig{mirror_self_recognition.jpg}{The mirror test: the moment an animal recognizes itself.
statements.section: VII. The Mirror on You

statements.quote: The whole enterprise — a frontier model trained to predict the next token — is, at its root, an act of *self-description*.
statements.section: VII. The Mirror on You

statements.quote: ML researchers built a machine out of the brain's own vocabulary and the brain's own laws, and pointed it at the record of the minds that made it.
statements.section: VII. The Mirror on You

statements.quote: It is a mirror made of mathematics, and the only face it has ever been trained on is a human one.
statements.section: VII. The Mirror on You

statements.quote: The first neural network was a brain.
statements.section: VII. The Mirror on You

statements.quote: The last word the machine has to learn is the one it has always been modeling: **you**.
statements.section: VII. The Mirror on You
